title: The Seljuks
hookLine: Turkish sultans who rule Persia and Anatolia and build the caravanserais

lines: A STONE GATE ON A PLATEAU.
cards: A stone gateway stands on a dry plateau in central Anatolia, taller than a house, carved with patterns as fine as lace. It looks like the entrance to a palace.
It was built for tired merchants and their animals, at the end of a long day on a road where the night is cold and not always safe.
Behind it: a courtyard with a well, a small mosque, stables for the animals, rooms for the people. The gate shuts at night, and inside, everyone sleeps.
Buildings like this still stand along the old roads, and some go back to one dynasty of Turkish sultans. Today: the Seljuks.

teach.b: The Seljuks began as a family of Turkish tribesmen from Central Asia, Muslims, who moved west with their horses and herds. In time they ruled much of Persia and Iraq.

When their leader Tughril entered Baghdad, the Abbasid caliph was still there, honored as the head of the Sunni world, but without real power. Tughril ruled with the title sultan, one who holds authority.

teach.h: THE CALIPH REIGNS, THE SULTAN RULES.
teach.b: So a new pattern took shape: the caliph as the symbol, the sultan as the ruler. Under the Seljuks, the vizier Nizam al-Mulk built the madrasahs you met earlier on this path.
Later, a branch of the family ruled Anatolia from the city of Konya, the land where Rumi would live and teach.
Along Anatolia's trade roads, the Seljuk sultans and their officials built caravanserais, road houses for travelers.
Some were paid for by endowments, so a traveler could rest without paying for the night, and the animals were fed too. Why spend fortunes in stone on strangers?
Trade, certainly: safe roads meant rich cities. But hospitality was also a duty of faith. The Qur'an names the wayfarer, the traveler on the road, among those who have a right to charity.

And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, links believing in God and the Last Day with honoring one's guest. A carved gate, a well, a mosque, a stable: faith built into a wall.

how: Muslims treat hospitality to guests and travelers as a religious duty, and Seljuk caravanserais in Turkey and Iran are visited today as monuments of that tradition.

games.q: you're a Seljuk sultan. you have wealth and builders. merchants cross your land on dangerous roads. what do you build?
o: walls to keep the merchants out.
games.why: the Seljuks and their officials built caravanserais along Anatolia's roads: safety for trade, and hospitality to the wayfarer.

practice: Think of one traveler in your own life: a friend driving in from far away, a new coworker, a delivery driver on a long shift. What would a road house look like for them, in your terms: a glass of water, a chair, a charger, a ride?
If you pray, you can ask for the safety of travelers.

wordCard.voice: The Seljuks. Turkish sultans who ruled Persia and Anatolia, kept the caliph as a symbol, and built road houses, caravanserais, for travelers. Today's word.
